summary: At 99 square miles, Malibu is physically larger than San Francisco yet holds fewer than 11,000 people — a density of just 107 per square mile, which means most of that vast footprint is Santa Monica Mountains parkland, canyon roads, and 21 miles of coastline rather than rooftops. That geography defines daily life: Pacific Coast Highway functions as the city's de facto main street and sole east-west artery, threading between ocean bluffs and steep chaparral-covered ridgelines, so a routine grocery run can become a scenic — or traffic-choked — event. With a median home value exceeding $2 million against a median household income around $192,000, the price-to-income ratio sits above 10:1, making even high earners heavily leveraged buyers; median rent above $3,500 a month reflects the same pressure on the rental side. Malibu is largely a bedroom community — Pepperdine University is the most prominent local employer, and entertainment and service-sector work accounts for much of the rest, so most career paths require the roughly 30-mile commute into greater Los Angeles. Year-round highs averaging 72°F with nine hours of daily sunshine and mild 58°F lows soften that tradeoff considerably, and trail access into the Santa Monica Mountains is essentially at the back door. The property-crime rate, however, runs notably high — larceny alone tops 2,900 per 100,000 — a figure worth weighing against the open, unenclosed character of many properties. Malibu is less a town you live *in* than a landscape you live *along*, with PCH as the single thread holding it all together.
